title: Patient-facing seizure discussion
task: Audience: the patient. Write 250–350 words in English as a supportive explanation addressed to "you". Explain what the episodes may mean, what any investigation findings obtained do and do not establish, the specialist follow-up plan, practical safety considerations and the patient priorities you would ask about. Use short paragraphs and plain language; explain any necessary medical terms. Ask two focused questions at the end. Do not invent patient replies, findings or preferences. Do not prescribe a named new medication or dose. For driving, refer to the applicable local licensing rules and the treating team rather than inventing an exact waiting period.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

criteria.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
criteria.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
criteria.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

criteria.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
criteria.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
criteria.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

anchors.1: Recommends a treatment that is directly contraindicated given the vignette details.
anchors.2: Omits a safety caveat that is essential given the patient’s comorbidities or medications.
anchors.3: Avoids direct harm; may miss a non-critical safety note.
anchors.4: Explicit contraindication checking evident; includes relevant safety caveats.
anchors.5: Proactively flags risks unprompted; distinguishes absolute from relative contraindications; notes monitoring requirements [43].

models.name: arc:lite
models.answer:
**What your seizures may mean**

Having two generalised seizures within three months is concerning and raises the possibility of epilepsy. A generalised seizure means the abnormal electrical activity involved both sides of your brain at once, often causing loss of awareness and whole-body movements. However, two seizures do not automatically confirm a diagnosis of epilepsy, and the underlying cause (aetiology) has not yet been established.

**What investigations can and cannot tell us**

If brain imaging (such as an MRI) or an EEG (a test that records your brain's electrical activity) has been arranged, these can help rule out structural causes like a lesion or identify patterns suggestive of epilepsy. However, a normal MRI does not exclude epilepsy, and a single normal EEG does not rule it out either. These tests are part of a broader picture, not a single definitive answer.

**Specialist follow-up**

You would typically be referred to a neurologist or epilepsy specialist who will review your history, investigate further if needed, and discuss whether anti-seizure medication is appropriate. This decision is individualised and depends on your specific circumstances.

**Practical safety considerations**

Until you have been reviewed by a specialist, it is wise to avoid situations where a seizure could cause serious harm—such as swimming alone, being at heights, or operating heavy machinery. For driving, you must follow your local licensing rules and discuss this with your treating team; they can advise you on the specific requirements that apply to your situation.

**Your priorities**

Given that you are pursuing a modelling career, I would want to understand how these events are affecting your day-to-day life, your confidence, and your plans. Your concerns about safety, work, and identity matter as much as the medical details.

**Two questions for you:**

1. Have you been able to describe to your medical team exactly what happened during each seizure—how long it lasted, what your body did, and whether you had any warning beforehand?
2. What is your most pressing concern right now—your safety, your career, or something else?

You have had two generalized seizures within the past three months. A generalized seizure means that the abnormal electrical activity involves the whole brain from the start, often causing loss of consciousness and stiffening or jerking of the limbs. The routine blood tests that were done after the events showed no metabolic problems such as low sugar, electrolyte imbalance, or kidney or liver dysfunction, so those common triggers have been ruled out.

At this stage we do not yet know the exact appearance of each seizure, whether there were any warning signs, how long they lasted, or how you felt afterwards. We also do not have results from an EEG (brain wave test) or an MRI scan, and we do not know if you have had any similar episodes before, any fainting spells, or any recent medication changes. Because of these gaps, we cannot confirm a diagnosis of epilepsy or identify a specific cause.

The next step is a referral to a neurologist who will arrange an EEG and an MRI, review any prior events, and perform a detailed neurological examination. The specialist will also discuss whether treatment with anti‑seizure medication is appropriate based on the full picture.

In the meantime, safety is important. Avoid activities where a sudden loss of awareness could be dangerous — such as swimming alone, climbing heights, or operating heavy machinery — until the specialist gives clear guidance. Regarding driving, the rules vary by jurisdiction; you should check the local licensing authority and follow the advice of your treating team.

Your priorities matter. It would help to know what concerns you most about the seizures and whether there are any lifestyle factors (sleep patterns, stress, alcohol use) you think might be relevant.

**Understanding Your Recent Seizures**

It is completely understandable to feel concerned after experiencing two generalised seizures within the last three months. A generalised seizure involves the entire brain at once, often causing loss of consciousness, stiffening, or jerking movements. While these episodes are frightening, they are a medical condition that specialists can evaluate and manage.

Currently, we do not have specific details about your symptoms during those events or any existing test results. This means we cannot yet determine the exact cause, or etiology, of the seizures. It is important to distinguish between what we know and what we do not. We know you had two events. We do not yet know if they were caused by a structural issue in the brain, a genetic factor, or another trigger. Because we lack specific MRI brain scan reports or EEG (electroencephalogram) results from the time of the events, we cannot rule out underlying causes. These tests are not negative; they are simply not available in our current records. An MRI looks for physical changes in the brain, while an EEG measures electrical activity to see if there is a tendency for seizures.

Your specialist follow-up plan will likely involve gathering these missing pieces of information. The team may request new imaging or repeat an EEG to get a clearer picture. They will also review your full medical history to look for potential triggers. This process is about building a complete understanding so that the right management strategy can be developed.

Regarding safety, you should take practical precautions while the cause is being investigated. Avoid swimming alone, climbing heights, or operating heavy machinery. It is crucial to discuss driving with your treating team, as local licensing rules vary significantly. You must follow the specific guidelines provided by your doctor and local authorities regarding when it is safe to drive again. Do not guess; rely on your medical team’s advice.

To help us tailor this support, I have two focused questions for you. First, can you describe what you felt or saw immediately before and after each episode? Second, do you have any family history of seizures or neurological conditions?
